problem: ROS 2/Nav2 indoor robots navigate to metric poses and cannot interpret intent-level language. VLM-based semantic navigation calls a slow VLM (2–9 s on consumer GPUs) for every instruction, forgets what it learned between sessions, and is rarely tested on physical multi-robot setups where learned semantic associations could be transferred between robots.
motivation: Most indoor instructions are unambiguous: they name a graph node, an object ID, an attribute or a single class. Running a multi-billion-parameter VLM on them wastes seconds, GPU time and camera bandwidth. Operator preferences resolved once by the VLM could be kept and reused deterministically, and shared by robots on the same map. The authors frame this as dual-process (System 1/System 2) reasoning, but with a training-free cascade in place of IROS's learned router.
key_idea: Put a 7-step deterministic, training-free resolver (graph names, object IDs, POI attributes, class/proximity, plus Jaccard matching against promoted memory preferences) before a VLM. Escalate to the VLM (Qwen 3.5:4b) only on ambiguity. Promote consistent VLM decisions into scoped memory (M1–M5) that is compiled into a shared ≤500-token digest, so other robots resolve those instructions deterministically in <0.1 ms.
insight: Once the environment has a navigation graph and hand-surveyed POIs with attributes, most semantic target selection reduces to lexical lookup. The VLM is needed only for affordance-level mappings (e.g., 'sit and relax' → radiator with seating=true), and those can be cached as operator preferences. Measurements: M3 preference resolution takes 0.065 ms versus 6,733 ms for VLM inference (~103,000×). Step 0 short-circuits the cascade, so it is also faster than Steps 1–6 (0.065 vs 0.213 ms, Mann–Whitney p<0.001). Navigation failures were unrelated to resolution method (Fisher p=0.563) and tracked AMCL drift (XY error 3.77 m on misses vs 0.30 m on successes), supporting evaluating L3 target choice separately from L1 execution. The inconsistent VLM outputs seen early in Session A came from YOLO false-positive chairs flooding the prompt; the authors fixed them at the perception layer by filtering dynamic detections in favour of static ones.
method: Semantic Autonomy Stack (SAS): six-layer reference framework (L0 platform, L1 Nav2 execution, L2 perception/semantic map from prior work, L3 reasoning, L4 mission interface, L5 memory) with fixed inter-layer interfaces.

L3a 7-step deterministic resolver: after normalization (lowercase, diacritics stripped, EN/RO), tries in order: Step 0 Jaccard match (≥0.6, unique node) to promoted M3 preferences; Step 1 regex node ID; Step 2 unique node-name substring; Step 3 unique POI obj_id; Step 4 lexical attribute-count scoring; Step 5 single class with a single instance; Step 6 proximity keyword + class → nearest instance by AMCL pose. Returns ESCALATE_TO_L3B if nothing is unambiguous.

L3b VLM reasoning: fetches a 640×480 camera frame over an HTTP bridge. Prompts Qwen 3.5:4b via Ollama (temp 0.3, think off) with a memory prefix, pose, the full graph, objects grouped by zone, a designated seating/resting block, and rules. Returns JSON {node_id, reason}.

Post-arrival confirmation routed by POI visual_signature_type: VLM checks landmark/contextual/architectural cues, or for 'none' POIs a pose-radius check (1.5 m). Logged separately and does not change mission outcome.

Executive contract ⟨A,O,V,L⟩ (adopted from ROSClaw): affordance manifest of nodes/POIs/allowed Nav2 actions; observation normalizer; validator (action allowlist, node exists, goal ≤50 m); JSONL audit logger with platform_id.

M1–M5 scoped memory + compiled digest: an offline extractor over audit logs builds M1 entity stats, M2 scene patterns, M3 instruction→node preferences, per-robot M4 capabilities and M5 task history. M3 is promoted when frequency ≥3, consistency ≥0.80 and at least one VLM resolution. A ≤2000-char digest is loaded read-only by all robots: M3 feeds L3a Step 0, M1/M2 feed the L3b prompt prefix.

setting.backbone: Qwen 3.5:4b VLM (frozen, served via Ollama on an RTX 5050 laptop) + rule-based 7-step deterministic resolver; YOLO26n for perception (L2, prior work)
setting.training_data: none (training-free); M3 preferences derived from runtime audit logs (15 seed VLM decisions on 3 instructions + earlier development sessions + Session A)
setting.observation: monocular RGB (Logitech C920, 640×480, fetched only on the VLM path) + 2D LiDAR + AMCL pose; VLM also receives textual navigation graph and semantic POI list
setting.action_space: selection of a target node on a 24-node / 60-edge navigation graph, executed by Nav2 (ComputeRoute/FollowPath/NavigateToPose/Spin with MPPI controller)
setting.privileged: pre-built occupancy map and hand-built navigation graph; 18 manually surveyed static POIs with semantic attributes (e.g., seating=true, use=resting spot) and visual-signature types; AMCL localization on known map

numbers_note: No standard embodied-navigation benchmark is used. All results come from a custom physical-robot protocol in one corridor (24-node graph, 18 POIs), and there are no quantitative baselines. The comparison to IROS/Hydra-Nav/etc. is qualitative only (Table 14). The claim that 10 of 82 decisions used L3b does not match Table 8/10, which list only 7 S3new L3b decisions.
results: On two Raspberry Pi 5 robots, the deterministic cascade resolved 72/82 scenario decisions (88%) without the VLM. All 33 M3-preference resolutions transferred from Xplorer-C to Xplorer-B hit the correct node (95% CI [0.894, 1.000]). Semantic accuracy on B was 41/41 while navigation completion was 36/41 (88%), with failures attributed to AMCL drift. The learned 'sit and relax' preference went from 6,733 ms of VLM inference (6/7 consistent) to 0.060–0.065 ms deterministic lookup, the reported ~103,000× speedup. There is no quantitative baseline; IROS's learned router (53.6% fast-path rate) is contrasted only qualitatively.
limitations: Tiny, single-environment, single-operator evaluation: one corridor, 24 nodes, 18 hand-surveyed POIs, and the same fixed phrasings reused. The 100% 'transfer accuracy' largely reflects exact-string Jaccard lookup of identical instructions, and the 88% fast-path rate reflects a test mix dominated by pre-promoted instructions.

M3 matching is lexical (Jaccard ≥0.6), so paraphrases with low overlap fail. Only one VLM (Qwen 3.5:4b) is tested and model-agnosticism is not verified empirically. VLM choices are non-deterministic (6/7 consistency).

Relies on manual POI annotation with attributes and on offline, manual memory refresh between sessions. Concurrent VLM escalation was never tested. The low camera cannot confirm wall-mounted targets (fire hydrant confirmation false on 10/10 runs).
